strengths: Novel threat formalization: First to formalize and investigate cross-modal interactive poisoning in MLLM-RecSys, identifying that fusion mechanisms designed for robustness can be exploited when perturbations are synchronized across modalities

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Rigorous testing across three datasets (Clothing, Sports, Toys), multiple settings (few-shot/zero-shot), extensive baselines (10 methods), and thorough ablation study demonstrating the necessity of each component
Strong empirical results: Achieves 0.73 mean ER@20 with +0.52 absolute improvement over strongest baseline while maintaining recommendation utility (HR and NDCG comparable to clean baseline)

Technically sound methodology: Pragmatic grey-box approach using surrogate proxy models; attention-guided saliency mining leverages model's own mechanisms; iterative co-adaptation with mask recomputation properly captures coupled nature of attack

Clear problem motivation and presentation: Figure 1 effectively contrasts attack paradigms; Definition 3.1 provides clean formal threat characterization; comprehensive experimental section with scaling analysis (poisoning ratio) and ablation studies
Practical relevance: Addresses emerging MLLM-RecSys systems with real implications for deployed recommendation platforms; demonstrates vulnerability even at minimal poisoning ratios (0.05%)
weaknesses: Limited victim model diversity: Primary experiments use only VIP5 (T5-small); T5-base relegated to appendix; no evaluation on other recent MLLM-RecSys (VL-CLIP, MISSRec, PMMRec, NoteLLM-2) mentioned in related work, limiting generalizability

Incomplete algorithmic specification: Visual perturbation via sign projection (Eq. 7) lacks justification; textual perturbation uses vague 'greedy search' and 'candidate set' without specifying size, composition, or fluency measurement; direction vector estimation ('probing small set') lacks detail on computational cost

Exposure Alignment assumptions not validated: Assumes high-exposure items share stable semantics across models without empirical verification; uses heuristic 'Best Sellers' anchor mining without robustness analysis; transferability of proxy model's representation space to victim model not empirically validated

Stealthiness constraints insufficiently rigorous: ROUGE-L ~90% and FID ~43 metrics lack perceptual validation (no human studies); novel cross-modal coherence metrics not compared against standard perceptual measures; no formal stealthiness guarantees or discussion of automated detection mechanisms

Missing robustness evaluation against defenses: Appendix section A.4 on defensive filtering deferred; no evaluation against practical defenses (content sanitization, anomaly detection, input perturbation); no evaluation against simple image transformations (JPEG compression, cropping, color jittering)

Gap between theory and practice: Bilevel optimization (Eq. 3) not actually solved; instead uses frozen proxy model heuristic; no analysis of approximation quality or proxy-victim transfer gap; could explain underperformance on unmeasured models

Insufficient statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; variance across runs not reported; counterintuitive finding (zero-shot outperforms few-shot) unexplained; results may lack statistical power

No proposed defenses or mitigation strategies: Paper identifies vulnerability but offers no solutions; inadequate ethics discussion despite demonstrating attack on deployed systems; lacks responsible disclosure considerations

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First to formally characterize cross-modal interactive poisoning against MLLM-RecSys, with clear insight that synchronized perturbations exploit consensus mechanisms originally designed for defense
Well-motivated attack: Figure 1 effectively illustrates why existing single-modality and interaction-level attacks fail, providing strong motivation for the proposed approach

Comprehensive experimental evaluation (within scope): Three datasets, ten baselines across three categories, Few-Shot/Zero-Shot settings, ablation studies, and multi-dimensional metrics (effectiveness, stealthiness, utility)
Strong empirical results: Substantial improvements over baselines (ER@20=0.73 mean, +0.52 over strongest baseline) while maintaining comparable recommendation utility (HR/NDCG)
Explicit stealthiness constraints: Thoughtful design incorporating both unimodal naturalness (ROUGE, FID) and cross-modal coherence requirements
Formal problem framework: Definition 3.1 provides clear mathematical formulation with well-defined attacker capabilities, constraints, and objectives
Reasonable threat model: Grey-box setting with public backbones as proxies is realistic and practical
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Individual components are standard techniques (attention rollout for saliency, sign projection for ℓ∞ perturbation, greedy token search). EA reduces to simple centroid averaging. Main contribution is iterative co-adaptation, which is more engineering than methodological innovation

Critical algorithmic details missing: How are direction vectors d^r computed exactly? How are text replacement candidates generated (BERT-MLM, embeddings, etc.)? Promised pseudocode in A.1 not provided. These omissions severely impact reproducibility

Extremely narrow victim model evaluation: Only VIP5 is the primary victim; T5-base in appendix only. No evaluation on other MLLM-RecSys architectures (MISSRec, PMMRec, NoteLLM-2, etc.) mentioned in related work. Claims about attacking 'MLLM-RecSys' broadly are not well-supported

Insufficient transferability analysis: Proxy model uses CLIP/T5 but victim may use different encoders. Limited evaluation of performance degradation under architecture mismatch, undermining grey-box threat model credibility

Questionable stealthiness claims: ROUGE-L scores ~92% and FID ~40 indicate substantial perturbations, not imperceptible ones. No qualitative examples, visualizations, or human evaluation. Cross-modal coherence improvements are marginal (0.0033 vs 0.0306 semantic consistency deviation)
No defense evaluation in main paper: Robustness against defenses deferred to appendix. This is critical for security research and should not be relegated to supplementary material
Limited to product recommendation only: All three datasets are Amazon reviews (Clothing, Sports, Toys). Generalization to other domains unclear. Scope too narrow for ICML

Inadequate ethical discussion: Impact statement says 'none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here' — unacceptable for security research. No responsible disclosure, no discussion of potential real-world harms to e-commerce platforms

Strong threat model assumptions: Requires adversary knowledge of high-exposure items, ability to inject UGC at scale (0.3-0.7% of users), and knowledge of victim using CLIP/T5. Practical feasibility and detectability not discussed

Unexplained phenomena undermine core claims: Zero-Shot ER@20 (0.7317) exceeds Few-Shot (0.7170), suggesting interaction poisoning dominates. Tab variant alone achieves ER@20=0.2669, and Tab+Img+Txt reaches 0.5617 (78% of full method), questioning whether cross-modal synchronization is truly the key mechanism

Missing critical experiments: No evaluation on diverse MLLM-RecSys architectures, no human evaluation of stealthiness, no anomaly detection analysis, no analysis of suspicious interaction patterns, no defense evaluation in main paper

Implementation clarity: Pre-extracted CLIP embeddings are unusual; unclear if they reflect victim model's actual embeddings. Hyperparameter choices (η, R, top-k) unjustified. Text candidate set generation unspecified. Multiple algorithmic details missing
Weak ablation interpretation: The contribution of attention-guided synchronization vs. simple multimodal perturbation is unclear when interaction poisoning alone achieves substantial ER@20

strengths: Novel problem formulation: First to formalize cross-modal interactive poisoning against MLLM-RecSys with clear insight that fusion mechanisms can amplify coordinated attacks rather than mitigate them
Strong experimental validation: Comprehensive evaluation across 3 datasets, 10 baselines, Few-Shot/Zero-Shot settings with consistent dominant performance (ER@20=0.73 vs. Shadowcast ~0.05)
Well-motivated insight: Figure 1 and Section 1 effectively explain why single-modality attacks fail while cross-modal approaches succeed on MLLM-RecSys
Rigorous problem formulation: Definition 3.1 clearly specifies threat model with explicit attacker knowledge, capabilities, constraints (stealthiness manifold B), and objectives
Thorough stealthiness evaluation: Dual dimensions of unimodal naturalness (ROUGE-L ~92%, FID ~36-43) and cross-modal coherence with direct validation (Semantic Consistency 0.0033 vs 0.0306)
Proper ablation study: Table 3 demonstrates cumulative contributions with critical 0.15 ER@20 leap from interactive co-adaptation, validating core hypothesis
Practical threat relevance: Maintains attack effectiveness at very low poisoning ratios (0.1-0.3%), addresses deployed systems (NoteLLM-2), and preserves recommendation utility
Attention-guided saliency mining: Clever technique leveraging cross-modal attention (Eq. 6) with iterative recomputation to enforce coupled perturbation nature
weaknesses: Incomplete appendix submission: Critical sections missing (A.1 algorithm details, A.4 defense robustness evaluation, A.5 multi-target details), severely limiting reproducibility assessment and security evaluation

Reproducibility concerns: Vague implementation details for gradient-free direction estimation ('small set of candidates' unspecified), text coherence thresholds ('significantly reduce' undefined), CIP termination conditions, and hyperparameter selection (η, ε, R, k)
Proxy model generalization unanalyzed: Uses public CLIP/T5 as fusion proxies without empirical validation of robustness to victim model architecture differences; T5-base results relegated to appendix
Unvalidated core assumption: Assumes high-exposure items share 'stable' semantic patterns across models (Section 4.2) without empirical support; lacks sensitivity analysis for EA robustness

Missing defense analysis: Defers robustness against defensive mechanisms to appendix; no proposed defenses or mitigation strategies; generic Impact Statement inadequate for security paper addressing real manipulation risks
Human evaluation absent: No perceptual evaluation of naturalness despite ROUGE drop to ~92% and FID scores 36-43 indicating potentially visible modifications; no detectability analysis
Incomplete technical analysis: No convergence guarantees for interactive loop, worst-case complexity bounds, or investigation of potential oscillation in CIP iterations
Limited scope: Only product recommendation (Amazon); unclear generalization to movies, music, or social content; category filtering sensitivity not explored

strengths: Novel problem formulation identifying cross-modal interactive poisoning against MLLM-RecSys, with the key insight that cross-modal consensus can amplify rather than mitigate coordinated attacks
Rigorous and comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 datasets, multiple victim models (VIP5 T5-small/base, DiffMM), and both Few-Shot and Zero-Shot settings with systematic ablations
Strong empirical results (ER@20=0.73, +0.52 over strongest baseline) while maintaining comparable recommendation utility (HR/NDCG), demonstrating effective targeted promotion with stealthiness
Well-motivated grey-box threat model requiring only public proxy models (CLIP, T5) without victim parameters, with low compromised-user ratio (0.1%) achieving measurable impact
Formal problem definition (Definition 3.1) with clear constraints, direct metrics validating core hypothesis (Semantic Alignment 0.0033 vs 0.0306), and thorough appendix with additional experiments
Effective ablation study demonstrating the critical role of cross-modal interaction (+0.15 ER@20 gap compared to non-interactive variants) and multi-target robustness over Shadowcast baseline
weaknesses: Reliance on surrogate model attention patterns transferring to victim models lacks theoretical justification; attention patterns may be unstable across fine-tuning strategies and architectures, and only two victim model families tested

Threat model realism concerns: assumes fine-tuning on specific users' poisoned UGC; modern platforms use online learning or batched updates; content moderation systems could detect perturbations; difficulty of account compromise at scale underexplored

Critical technical details underspecified: visual perturbation candidate sampling procedure undefined; textual candidate sampling size unspecified; computational costs not reported; direction estimation vague (Algorithm 1 line 15)

Stealthiness claims benefit from scrutiny: ROUGE-L scores of 89-92 not exceptional; FID scores of 36-43 indicate visible changes; Semantic Alignment only compared against clean baseline (0.0306) providing weak reference; Freq-Rarity defense reduces ER@20 by ~11% showing non-trivial defense effectiveness; no human evaluation

Limited defense evaluation with only three basic defenses tested; missing certified robustness, adversarial training, embedding-level anomaly detection; no proposed defenses despite identifying vulnerability

Incomplete ablation study lacking hyperparameter sensitivity (k for top-k, ε for perturbation budget, R for iterations, early-stopping threshold); visual-textual perturbation dependencies not cleanly isolated; lower ER@20 on T5-base (0.4850 vs 0.7170) suggests model-size dependence not deeply analyzed

strengths: Novel problem formulation: identifies that cross-modal consensus, typically a defense mechanism, becomes a vulnerability under synchronized perturbations—a genuine insight for MLLM-RecSys security

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 diverse datasets (e-commerce, short-video) with 10 baselines, ablation studies, multi-target scenarios, and transferability analysis (T5-base, DiffMM, MicroLens)
Strong empirical results: achieves mean ER@20 of 0.73 with +0.52 absolute improvement over strongest baseline while maintaining comparable recommendation utility (HR, NDCG)
Formal threat model definition with explicit stealthiness constraints and bilevel optimization formulation (Def. 3.1, Eq. 3)
Effective ablation study (Table 4) demonstrating the critical importance of cross-modal interaction (ER@20: 0.5617 → 0.7170)
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: combines straightforward existing techniques (centroid averaging for EA, attention rollout for saliency, sign-based perturbation, greedy token replacement) without significant innovation or theoretical insight

Critical algorithmic details are severely underspecified: (1) 'Gradient-free direction estimation' (Alg. 1, line 15) via 'probing candidate perturbations' lacks specifics on candidate generation and selection; (2) Stealthiness thresholds for 'significantly reduce semantic consistency' never defined; (3) Normalization choice in Eq. 4 unjustified

Insufficient defense evaluation: only 3 basic defenses tested (adapted from prior work, not designed for multimodal systems); no evaluation against defenses targeting synchronized perturbations or certified robustness approaches; ER@20 ≥ 0.6357 under defenses but no analysis of whether this is acceptable

Shallow mechanistic understanding: paper claims cross-modal fusion amplifies malicious signals but provides only empirical evidence, not analysis of why synchronization helps—could be simply more optimization rather than fundamental fusion vulnerability

Questionable threat model assumptions: (1) assumes access to publicly observable high-exposure item lists not validated across platforms; (2) requires simultaneous control of text and images, potentially breakable through independent validation; (3) proxy model (CLIP+T5) validity as surrogate for victim's ΦΘ not theoretically justified or sensitivity-tested; (4) 0.1% compromised user ratio realism unvalidated

Inadequate ethical treatment: Impact Statement (Section 6) dismisses discussion of societal consequences, no responsible disclosure discussion, no assessment of practical attack likelihood or existing mitigations in deployed systems

Reproducibility concerns: underspecified implementation details (random seeds, exact convergence criteria, candidate sampling), missing human evaluation of stealthiness despite claiming perturbations remain 'inconspicuous', no validation that ROUGE/FID metrics correlate with imperceptibility

Insufficient analysis of failure modes and generalization: attack tested only on bottom-20% items (cold-start scenario); no analysis of performance on arbitrary/popular items; no discussion of sensitivity to model architecture, training procedure, or architectural variations

Presentation issues: (1) notation inconsistencies (D̃mal vs. D̃_mal); (2) ⊕ operator never formally defined; (3) counter-intuitive Zero-Shot > Few-Shot results (ER@20: 0.7170 → 0.7317) inadequately explained despite deserving deeper investigation; (4) overclaiming 'first to formalize' for empirical study

Limited defenses and no proposed countermeasures: paper does not propose or theoretically analyze what properties a defense against synchronized cross-modal attacks should have; focuses only on attack demonstration without contributing to defense landscape

strengths: Novel identification and formalization of cross-modal interactive poisoning vulnerability in MLLM-RecSys, with compelling insight that multimodal consensus amplifies rather than mitigates coordinated attacks

Rigorous and comprehensive experimental evaluation across 4 datasets, 10 baselines, multiple victim models (VIP5 T5-small/base, DiffMM), and both Few-Shot/Zero-Shot settings with extensive ablation studies

Sound methodological design with two complementary components (Exposure Alignment leveraging observable signals, Cross-modal Interactive Perturbation with attention-guided saliency) that cleanly decompose the attack
Strong empirical results demonstrating mean ER@20=0.73 with +0.52 absolute improvement over strongest baseline while maintaining recommendation utility (HR/NDCG comparable to clean baseline)

Comprehensive stealthiness evaluation including novel cross-modal coherence metrics (Semantic Alignment, Latent Direction Alignment) demonstrating coordinated rather than independent perturbations, with ROUGE-L~90% text fluency and FID~42 visual plausibility
Thorough hyperparameter and scaling analysis showing effectiveness at minimal poisoning budgets (0.05%) and robustness against multiple defenses (ER@20≥0.64 even with Freq-Rarity defense)
Clear, well-organized presentation with effective visual explanations and comprehensive appendix supporting reproducibility through detailed algorithms, hyperparameters, and implementation details
weaknesses: Stealthiness constraints B defined intuitively rather than formally; unimodal naturalness and cross-modal coherence constraints validated post-hoc empirically rather than enforced a priori with explicit mathematical specifications

Gradient-free direction estimation (Eq. 7) under-specified: number of candidate perturbations, their sampling distribution, and computational cost not detailed—a critical component deserving rigorous specification

Gradient-free visual perturbation relies on limited candidates which may lead to suboptimal directions; no analysis of convergence properties or theoretical guarantees for the interactive optimization loop

Surrogate-based attack using public CLIP/T5 models creates transferability gap with actual victim models; while T5-base and DiffMM transfers partially address this, no detailed analysis of proxy-victim similarity effects on success

Limited ethical discussion for a sensitive topic: Impact Statement dismissively states 'none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted,' but poisoning attacks on recommendations raise explicit concerns about malicious content promotion, fraud facilitation, and user trust—more substantive discussion warranted

Defense evaluation limited to simple baselines; no evaluation against adaptive defenses specifically targeting cross-modal inconsistency or directional alignment, and no discussion of developing next-generation defenses
Missing failure mode analysis: no discussion of when/why attacks fail, how item semantic distance from high-exposure regions affects success, or what item properties resist promotion

Textual perturbation details underspecified: exact threshold for 'significantly reduce' semantic consistency (Section 4.3) not defined, number of candidate tokens sampled not stated, integration with visual state during optimization unclear
